title: The second sight: a sick man
hookLine: a man shaking with fever by the road; and this too, he asks
tomorrow: the third sight: a dead man
last: CHANNA — THIS IS COMING FOR ALL OF US.

lines: THE MORNING YOU WAKE UP SICK.
A MAN SHAKING BY THE ROAD.
cards: Something is off the moment you wake. A scratch in the throat, a heaviness behind the eyes. Yesterday you had plans.
Today the plans belong to the fever. The stories say the prince went out a second time. The king had doubled the guards and the music, hoping to keep his son's mind on pleasure.
Channa drove the chariot out again, down a road swept clean. And by the side of it lay a man shaking with fever, too weak to stand, being helped up by others.
The prince looked, and asked the question again, a little quieter this time.

teach.b: What's wrong with him, the prince asks. Channa tells him: this man is sick. And again the question: can this happen to me?
And again the plain answer: nobody is beyond sickness. The first sight was about time, the slow bending of age. This one is sharper.
Sickness doesn't wait for old age. It can arrive at twenty, at five, on a Tuesday, in the middle of your plans. The prince had thought of his body as his, the way a palace was his.
The fever by the road said otherwise. Years later, the Buddha put it in one line.
This body, he told his monks, isn't yours, and it doesn't belong to anyone else either. It's the result of old causes, something to be seen clearly, not owned. The body is borrowed.
Not a prison, not a possession. A loan, looked after for a while, returned in the end. And the Buddha lived what he taught.

teach.h: AN OLD CART HELD WITH STRAPS.
teach.b: Near the end of his life, sick and in pain, he told his friend Ananda that his body was like an old cart that keeps going only because it's held together with straps.
He didn't pretend. He didn't despair either. Buddhists say this is the point: to see sickness as it is, without the extra layer of shock, why me, how dare you.
The fever is real. The outrage is the part you might be able to set down.

how: The five remembrances Buddhists reflect on include being subject to illness, and in some traditions monks visit and chant for the sick.

o: A vow of silence kept by monks

games.q: what's inside the second sight — tap the pairs.
p: an old cart held with straps
the Buddha's body near the end

s: the Buddha taught that the body is a prison to escape
he called it not yours and not another's: something to see clearly, not hate or own.
near the end of his life the Buddha compared his body to an old cart
an old cart kept going only by being held together with straps.
sickness in the story comes only to the old
the second sight is a lesson that illness can come at any age.

games.q: you're Channa. the prince points at a man shaking with fever and asks if this can happen to him. what do you say?
o: no, not to someone like you.
games.why: Channa tells the truth again: nobody is beyond sickness. the plain answer is what sets everything in motion.

practice: Settle into your seat and look for one small ache: a stiff neck, a sore knee, tired eyes. Rest your attention on it gently, the way you'd rest a hand on a friend's shoulder.

Notice it without the story, not 'this always happens,' not 'why won't it stop,' just the sensation itself: warm, tight, dull, moving. If the ache changes, let it; if your mind runs off, come back to it.

wordCard.voice: Vyādhi. Sickness, the Pali word for the fever that stops the prince on the road and comes to everyone, at any age, without asking.

orig.note: Pali: sickness, disease (also vyādhi). The second of the sights.

carryVoice: Your line: the body is borrowed. Nobody owns one outright, not even a prince. Until tomorrow.
